name: Darjeeling
tagline: Tea gardens, the toy train and Kangchenjunga from the ridge
summary: The Darjeeling hills rise from Siliguri in the plains to Darjeeling town at about 2,045 m and Sandakphu at 3,636 m, the highest point in West Bengal. Come for the toy train, the tea estates, sunrise on Kangchenjunga and the Singalila ridge trek. October to December and March to May are the best months.
meta_description: Plan Darjeeling, Kurseong, Mirik, Tiger Hill and Sandakphu on a budget: toy train, tea estates, best months, costs, routes from Siliguri, NJP and Bagdogra.
intro: The Darjeeling hills climb steeply out of the plains of north Bengal. In two or three hours by road you go from Siliguri, at about 120 m, through forest and tea gardens to Kurseong at 1,480 m and Darjeeling at 2,045 m. To the north, across deep valleys, Kangchenjunga fills the sky on clear days; to the west, the Singalila ridge marks the border with Nepal.

This is tea country. More than eighty estates grow Darjeeling tea on these slopes, from Makaibari near Kurseong to Happy Valley just below Darjeeling town. The Darjeeling Himalayan Railway, a 2 ft gauge line opened in 1881 and listed by UNESCO in 1999, still climbs 88 km from NJP to Darjeeling, and its steam joy rides to Ghum are one of the region's great pleasures.

The region suits most travellers. Families come for the toy train, the zoo and the easy walks of Mirik. Couples come for heritage hotels and tea-garden stays. Trekkers walk the Singalila ridge to Sandakphu for a view of Everest and Kangchenjunga together. Budget travellers find shared jeeps, family guesthouses and cheap, good food. Comfort travellers have heritage hotels and tea-estate bungalows to choose from.

Distances are short but roads are slow, steep and often foggy, so allow more time than the kilometres suggest. Plan around the weather: clear skies from October to December, flowers and first-flush tea in spring, cold but bright winters and a wet, cloudy monsoon from June to September. A shared jeep from Siliguri to Darjeeling, for example, takes about three hours for 65 km.

highlights.title: The toy train
highlights.text: Ride the UNESCO-listed Darjeeling Himalayan Railway from Darjeeling to Ghum by steam, past the Batasia Loop.

highlights.title: Tea estates
highlights.text: Walk and taste at Happy Valley, Makaibari and the gardens around Mirik, or sleep on a working estate.

highlights.title: Tiger Hill sunrise
highlights.text: Watch first light on Kangchenjunga, with Everest on the far horizon on the clearest mornings.

highlights.title: The Sandakphu trek
highlights.text: Walk the Singalila ridge to 3,636 m for a view of four of the world's five highest peaks.

highlights.title: Monasteries and temples
highlights.text: Visit Ghum Monastery, founded in 1850, Bokar Monastery in Mirik and the shared Hindu-Buddhist shrine on Observatory Hill.

highlights.title: Quiet hill towns
highlights.text: Slow down in Kurseong and Mirik, warmer and calmer than Darjeeling and close to the plains.

facts: Nepali, Bengali, Hindi, English; also Lepcha, Tibetan and other community languages
None for Darjeeling; park entry and a licensed guide for the Sandakphu trek
people: Most people in the Darjeeling hills are Nepali-speaking Gorkhas, whose communities include Rai, Limbu, Tamang, Gurung, Magar, Newar, Sherpa, Chhetri and Bahun families, many descended from those who came to build the town and work the tea gardens in the 19th century. The Lepchas are the earliest inhabitants, and Bhutia, Tibetan and Yolmo families add Buddhist traditions. Nepali is the common language of the hills, while Siliguri in the plains is largely Bengali-speaking with Marwari, Bihari and Nepali communities. Hindu, Buddhist and Christian festivals are all kept, often by the same neighbourhoods, and many families have long served in the Gorkha regiments.

budget_day.covers: per person per day: a shared room in a family guesthouse, shared jeeps between towns, local cafés and momo shops, one paid sight such as the zoo or a tea tasting
per person per day: a good mid-range hotel with views, a reserved car for sightseeing, restaurant meals, the toy train joy ride and entry fees
per person per day: a heritage hotel or tea-estate bungalow with meals, a private car and driver for the whole trip, steam joy ride and guided tea visits

months.summary: The coldest month, with crisp skies and the best chances of clear Kangchenjunga views. Crowds are thin and hotel prices low. Snow is rare in Darjeeling town but common at Sandakphu.
months.tip: Book a room with a heater and pack thermals; Tiger Hill at dawn is below freezing.

months.summary: Still cold but brightening, with long clear spells. Tibetan and Sherpa families celebrate Losar, and monasteries hang new prayer flags. Sandakphu may still have snow on the track.
months.tip: Check the Losar date for the year and visit Ghum Monastery during the new year prayers.

months.weather: Mild days, cool nights, 7–15°C in Darjeeling
months.summary: Spring begins and the first-flush tea is plucked. Rhododendrons start to flower lower down. Haze can soften the views later in the month, but the weather is pleasant for walking.
months.tip: Visit a tea factory in late March for first-flush processing and tastings.

months.weather: Warm, some haze and afternoon showers, 10–17°C
months.summary: A fine month for the Singalila ridge, with rhododendrons flowering on the way to Sandakphu. Towns are pleasant, though afternoon clouds often hide the mountains.
months.tip: Start walks and drives early; clouds and showers usually build after midday.

months.weather: Mild in the hills, hot in Siliguri, 12–19°C in Darjeeling
months.summary: Peak holiday season as the plains heat up. Second-flush tea begins. Darjeeling is busy and prices rise; book hotels and toy train seats early.
months.tip: Book the steam joy ride on IRCTC weeks ahead for May dates.

months.summary: The monsoon usually arrives in early to mid-June. School holidays keep Darjeeling busy early in the month, but views fade and roads see the first landslides. Singalila National Park traditionally closes to trekkers from mid-June.
months.tip: Leave a spare day for road delays. Check current status before you travel.

months.summary: The wettest time of year. Tea gardens are green and quiet, but mountain views are rare and roads and the toy train can be disrupted by landslides.
months.tip: Choose Kurseong or Mirik for a cheap, misty break, and travel by day only.

months.summary: Rain continues with breaks. Hotel prices are at their lowest. Leeches appear on forest paths. Good for travellers who like mist and empty roads rather than views.
months.tip: Carry an umbrella and leech socks for any forest walk.

months.summary: The monsoon fades through the month and the first clear mornings return late in September. Durga Puja and Dashain may fall at the end of the month in some years, bringing crowds.
months.tip: Check the Puja dates for your year and book early if they fall in September.

months.summary: The best month for views, and the busiest. Durga Puja, Dashain and Tihar fill the hills with holidaymakers. Sandakphu reopens for trekkers after the monsoon break.
months.tip: Book hotels, cars and the toy train six to eight weeks ahead.

months.summary: Clear skies, autumn-flush tea and fewer crowds once the festival holidays end. One of the best months for the Sandakphu trek and Tiger Hill.
months.tip: Pack a warm jacket; nights get cold quickly after mid-November.

months.summary: Crisp, clear days and long views, with Christmas and New Year bringing a short rush. Mirik's oranges are ripe. Sandakphu is cold and may get its first snow.
months.tip: Book Christmas week early; the rest of the month is quiet and cheap.

getting_there: Bagdogra airport (IXB), 14 km from Siliguri, has flights from Delhi, Kolkata, Mumbai, Bengaluru and other cities. New Jalpaiguri (NJP), 6 km from Siliguri, is the main railway station, with trains from Kolkata, Delhi and Guwahati. From Siliguri, Darjeeling is about 65 km and 3–3.5 hours by road via Rohini and Kurseong, Kurseong 34 km and 1.5–2 hours, and Mirik 52 km and 2–2.5 hours. Shared jeeps leave from the stands near the Tenzing Norgay Central Bus Terminus on Hill Cart Road and from NJP; reserved cars are available at NJP and Bagdogra prepaid counters. The toy train runs from NJP to Darjeeling in about 7–8 hours.
permits: Indians and foreigners need no permit to visit Darjeeling, Kurseong, Mirik or Tiger Hill. For Sandakphu, everyone pays the Singalila National Park entry fee at Manebhanjan and carries photo ID, and trekkers must hire a licensed guide. The trail crosses into Nepal in places, where ID is checked. Foreigners continuing to Sikkim need an Inner Line Permit, available in Siliguri or at Rangpo. Fees and rules change. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: How many days do I need for Darjeeling?
faqs.a: Allow four to seven days. Three nights in Darjeeling covers Tiger Hill, the toy train, tea gardens, the zoo and the town. Add a night in Kurseong or Mirik for a quieter stop, and five or six days for the Sandakphu trek. With a week you can combine Darjeeling with Kalimpong or Gangtok, both 2–4 hours away.

faqs.q: What is the best time to visit Darjeeling?
faqs.a: October to December gives the clearest mountain views and dry weather. March to May brings spring flowers and first- and second-flush tea, with warmer days but more haze. January and February are cold and clear. Avoid June to September if you want views; the monsoon brings cloud, heavy rain and road disruptions.

faqs.q: How do I get from NJP or Bagdogra to Darjeeling?
faqs.a: Take a shared jeep from NJP or the Siliguri stands near the Tenzing Norgay Central Bus Terminus for about ₹250–350 a seat, 3–3.5 hours, or a reserved car from the prepaid counters for about ₹2,800–3,800. The toy train from NJP takes 7–8 hours. From Bagdogra, the drive to Darjeeling is about 3 hours.

It can be done cheaply. Budget travellers spend about ₹1,800–2,800 a day on family guesthouses, shared jeeps and local food. A Value trip with good hotels and a private car costs about ₹4,000–6,500 per person a day. Prices rise by 20–40 percent in October, May and the Christmas week, so travel outside those weeks to save money.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit for Darjeeling?
faqs.a: No. Darjeeling, Kurseong, Mirik and Tiger Hill need no permit for Indians or foreigners. Sandakphu needs a national park entry fee, photo ID and, for trekkers, a licensed guide. Foreigners going on to Sikkim need an Inner Line Permit, arranged in Siliguri or at the Rangpo border. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Is the toy train worth it?
faqs.a: Yes, but choose the right ride. The two-hour joy ride from Darjeeling to Ghum and back, ideally by steam, gives you the Batasia Loop, the Ghum museum and the best of the line for ₹1,000–1,800. The full NJP to Darjeeling journey takes 7–8 hours and suits rail lovers with a full day to spare. Book on IRCTC in advance.

faqs.q: Should I stay in Darjeeling, Kurseong or Mirik?
faqs.a: Darjeeling has the most sights, views and food, and suits a first visit of three nights. Kurseong is quieter, warmer and closer to NJP, good for tea gardens and a first or last night. Mirik is calm and family-friendly around its lake. Many travellers combine Darjeeling with one night in either of the smaller towns.

faqs.q: Can I combine Darjeeling with Sikkim?
faqs.a: Yes, easily. Gangtok is about 95–100 km and 4–5 hours from Darjeeling via the Teesta valley, Pelling about 70–80 km and 4–5 hours via Jorethang, and Kalimpong about 50 km and 2.5 hours. Foreigners need a Sikkim Inner Line Permit, which can be issued at the Melli or Rangpo border posts. Allow at least seven days for a combined trip.

faqs.q: Is Darjeeling good for a family holiday?
faqs.a: Yes. The toy train, the zoo with red pandas and snow leopards, pony rides on Chowrasta, tea gardens and Mirik's lake suit children. Choose a hotel with car access, as Darjeeling's lanes are steep. Pack warm clothes even in May. Avoid the monsoon and plan early nights before Tiger Hill dawn starts.
